affiliate-commission-on-returns.html.text:
← TikTok Shop Fee Calculator

A 15% affiliate and a 12% return rate on the same $19.99 SKU

“TikTok Shop takes 6%” is true and incomplete. The number that decides whether a creator listing makes money is usually the commission you set, times the share of orders that come back without clawing that commission back.

The SKU

A $19.99 beauty item. The buyer pays no postage. It cost $5.50 to buy, $4.28 to fulfill, $0.40 to pack, and $1.50 of ads are allocated to the order. Referral is the mid-2026 US default of 6%. You offer creators 15% of item price. 12% of orders come back. 80% of those returned units cannot be sold again. The creator keeps the commission on a return.

If the order is kept

Illustrative rates. Yours depend on category, region, and the commission you actually set.
Buyer paid$19.99
TikTok referral, 6%−$1.20
Creator commission, 15%−$3.00
Item, fulfill, pack, ads−$11.68
You keep$4.11

That looks fine. A seller who stops here raises the commission to get more creators on the SKU.

If the order comes back

The buyer is refunded. TikTok typically returns most of the referral and keeps a refund-admin fee (20% of that referral, capped at $5). The outbound fulfillment, packaging, and ads have already been spent. In this example 80% of the $5.50 item is unsellable. The $3.00 creator commission stays with the creator.

Refund to the buyer$0.00 kept
Refund admin (20% of $1.20)−$0.24
Creator commission, not clawed back−$3.00
Unsellable goods (80% of $5.50)−$4.40
Outbound fulfill, pack, ads−$6.18
You lose$13.82

Expected value at a 12% return rate

88% of the time you keep $4.11. 12% of the time you lose $13.82. Expected profit is $1.96 — less than half of the “kept order” figure, and a 9.8% margin on the revenue you actually retain. The same SKU sold organically (no creator cut) expects about $5.00. The affiliate path costs roughly $3.04 more per order after returns, almost the entire 15% you offered.

Open the calculator and change the return rate or the claw-back toggle. The gap is the product: a listing that looks profitable at 6% + 15% is a different listing once returns keep the commission.

What the announced 1 October 2026 rates do to this SKU

Under the announced 8% referral plus 1.5% creator facilitation on affiliate-sourced orders, the same affiliate path keeps about $1.36 instead of $1.96. That is still not a pricing recommendation — it is the arithmetic on these assumptions. Confirm the live schedule in Seller Center before you reprice.

Common questions

Does a TikTok Shop affiliate commission still cost you on a returned order?

Usually yes. In the worked example the creator keeps the 15% commission when the order comes back, TikTok returns most of the 6% referral but keeps a refund-admin fee, and the outbound fulfillment, packaging, and ads are already spent. A kept order leaves $4.11 and a returned order loses $13.82.

What is the real margin on a 15% affiliate SKU at a 12% return rate?

Expected profit is $1.96 per order, not the $4.11 a kept order shows, because 88% of the time you keep $4.11 and 12% of the time you lose $13.82. That is a 9.8% margin on the revenue you actually retain. The same SKU sold organically with no creator cut expects about $5.00.

No warranty. This page is free arithmetic on a worked example, not tax, financial, or business advice. Verify every figure against your own statements and a qualified professional before relying on it.

Nothing on this page is uploaded anywhere. It is a static document.

Common questions

How much does TikTok Shop take per sale?

US shops usually pay a unified referral fee of about 6% of the fee base (customer payment plus platform discount minus tax). That rate already covers payment processing on domestic orders. Creator commissions you set, Fulfilled by TikTok or your own postage, ads, and returns stack on top. This page does the arithmetic from the rates you enter; it does not publish TikTok's live schedule.

Do I still pay affiliate commission if the buyer returns the order?

Often yes. Many sellers report the creator keeps the commission on a returned order. This calculator defaults to that. Tick 'affiliate commission is clawed back on a return' if your own statements show otherwise. Combined with a double-digit return rate, that is how a listing that looks fine at 6% loses money.

What changes on 1 October 2026?

TikTok has announced a move from a 6% standard US referral to 8% on most categories, plus a 1.5% creator facilitation fee on affiliate-sourced orders. This page compares your SKU under the mid-2026 defaults and under that announced schedule. Status check, 16 October 2026: that date has now passed, and the sources found while checking disagree. Several third-party seller guides say the 8% referral took effect on 4 August 2026, TikTok's public fee table was reported still showing 6%, and no source found mentions the 1.5% facilitation fee. Treat both schedules as scenarios and verify the live numbers in Seller Center and on your settlement statements before you reprice.

should-i-bundle-tiktok-shop-orders.html.text:
TIKTOK SHOP · BUNDLE DISCOUNT

The discount has to beat one saved order, not two sales.

A "buy 2, save X%" deal only avoids the per-order costs a second checkout would repeat — referral, creator commission, product cost, and ad spend all scale with units either way. This page compares a bundle against selling the same units as separate full-price orders, and solves for the discount that still matches them. Back to the full calculator.

The bundle

Bundle vs separate orders

Path Price Expected leftover

Transparent arithmetic from your inputs — not a ranking, a conversion forecast, or advice about what discount to run.

Common questions

Should I offer a bundle discount on TikTok Shop?

On the calculator example — a $19.99 item, 6% referral, 15% creator commission, 12% returns — a 2-pack at 10% off keeps $2.30 less than two separate full-price orders ($1.62 vs $3.92). Bundling only saves the flat per-order costs a second checkout would repeat (packaging and other per-order costs here), and a 10% price cut spends far more than that saves. Dropping the discount to about 1.5% would match selling the two units separately.

Why would bundling ever beat two separate orders?

Because some costs are charged once per order regardless of how many units are on it — a payment processor's flat fee, packaging, or any other per-order cost — while referral, creator commission, product cost, and ad spend all scale with units either way. A bundle at 0% discount keeps exactly those saved per-order costs; on the calculator defaults that is $0.40 more than two separate orders. Any real discount has to beat that number, not the other way around.

What discount can I offer without losing money on a bundle?

The page solves for it: the discount percentage at which the bundle's expected leftover exactly equals selling the same units separately. On the calculator example that ceiling is about 1.5% — well short of a typical "buy 2 save 10%" offer. Replace the rates and costs with your own SKU to get your own ceiling; it moves with referral rate, commission, and how large your genuinely per-order costs are.

The badge is not a fee-base tie when creators are paid on the item.

TikTok’s referral sits on item price plus shipping charged, so $19.99 + $4.99 and $24.98 + $0.00 take the same referral. Creator commission usually does not. Common questions

Should I offer free shipping on TikTok Shop?

On the calculator example — a $19.99 item, $4.99 shipping charged, 6% referral, 15% creator commission on item price only, 12% returns — charging shipping keeps more than baking the $4.99 into the item. Referral is a tie (same fee base). Affiliate is not: the creator is paid on the higher item price. Eating the label at $19.99 drops leftover further and needs extra orders to match.

Is moving shipping into the item price free on TikTok Shop?

No when commission is on item price only. TikTok's referral sits on item plus shipping charged, so $19.99 + $4.99 and $24.98 + $0.00 take the same referral. The creator payout rises by 15% of the $4.99 you moved. Tick 'commission includes shipping charged' if your own statements already pay creators on the full customer total — then the same customer total is a leftover tie.

Does free shipping need extra orders to stay even?

Yes when leftover per order falls. The page shows how many extra orders per month would match charging shipping. If the free-shipping path has a non-positive leftover, extra volume cannot catch up.

vs-tiktok-shops-seller-university.html.text:
← TikTok Shop fee calculator

This calculator vs. TikTok Shop's own Seller University fee pages

TikTok Shop publishes its standing fee policy for US sellers through its Seller University knowledge base: a referral fee that runs about 6% of the fee base for most categories, calculated from the customer's payment plus any platform-funded discount and minus tax — not from what eventually lands in a seller's bank account. On a return, TikTok's own Returns and Refunds policy refunds the referral fee back to the seller minus a refund administration fee of 20% of that referral fee, capped at $5 per SKU since 15 May 2025. That schedule and policy are free to read for any seller and are the right place to check what a stated rate currently is.

After an order has shipped, TikTok's own Finance & Settlement pages in Seller Center itemize what was actually withheld from a payout — a real, useful, and free resource, but a retrospective one: it reports what a sale already cost, not what a listing decision in front of you will cost. Neither of TikTok's own resources is a standalone what-if calculator a seller can run before listing.

Between a schedule that states rates and a statement that reports what already happened sits the arithmetic on decisions still open: does an affiliate listing beat an organic one once the creator's commission is paid, does that commission still get paid when the buyer returns the order, what list price breaks even or hits a target margin, what does a bundle discount cost against selling the same units separately, and what does TikTok's own announced 1 October 2026 move to an 8% referral fee plus a 1.5% creator facilitation fee on affiliate-sourced orders do to all of the above on the same SKU. This calculator does not try to reproduce TikTok's rate card as a stored table — every fee here is a box you type from your own Seller Center numbers, so it never drifts out of date the way a hard-coded schedule would, and TikTok's published rates can change without this page needing an update.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or TikTok's own Seller University fee pages?

Both, for different jobs. TikTok Shop's Seller University knowledge base publishes the standing policy: the referral fee schedule by category, how the fee base is defined (customer payment plus any platform-funded discount, minus tax), and the refund administration fee taken back on a return (20% of the referral fee refunded, capped at $5 per SKU since 15 May 2025). It is the right place to check what a stated rate currently is. It does not compare an organic listing against paying a creator commission, does not price a return where the creator keeps their commission anyway, does not compute a break-even or target-margin list price, and does not put today's rates beside TikTok's own announced 1 October 2026 schedule on the same order. This calculator does not try to reproduce TikTok's rate card as a stored table — every rate here is a box you type — and instead runs the seven decisions the schedule itself leaves open.

Does TikTok Shop have its own interactive fee calculator?

Not that TikTok publishes for sellers to use ahead of a listing. Seller University states the fee schedule and policy in prose and tables, and the Seller Center's own finance and settlement pages itemize what was actually withheld after an order has already shipped and any return window has passed. Neither is a standalone what-if tool: seeing what a hypothetical order nets before you list it, with a creator commission that survives a return, is the gap this calculator fills.

vs-tracking-it-in-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← TikTok Shop fee calculator

TikTok Shop Fee Calculator vs. tracking it in a spreadsheet

A seller who prices more than one TikTok Shop listing usually ends up with a spreadsheet: a cell for the referral rate, one for the creator commission, a note somewhere that the commission is not clawed back on a return, and a second copy of the whole sheet the week the announced 1 October 2026 schedule needs comparing against today's. Each formula is ordinary arithmetic. Keeping them right — especially the commission-survives-a-return rule, which is the one detail a generic "TikTok takes 6%" page or a rushed spreadsheet formula is most likely to get backwards — is the part that gets skipped when a listing needs a price today.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can reproduce every formula this calculator runs — the referral fee on the fee base, an affiliate commission held back from the seller's net but kept by the creator on a return, the facilitation fee that applies only to affiliate-sourced orders, and a break-even or target-margin price. Building it means reading the current rates off Seller University, encoding the commission-survives-a-return rule correctly, and adding a second block of formulas to hold the announced October schedule beside today's on the same order.

This calculator keeps the organic-versus-affiliate split, the return rate, and both fee schedules on one screen, already wired to the presets in the calculator. A shareable link carries the full scenario in the URL, and the fee-change page and returns page work a full example through the arithmetic this page only describes.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet do this math instead?

Yes. Every formula this calculator runs — the referral fee on the fee base, an affiliate commission that is not clawed back when the order is returned, the creator facilitation fee on affiliate-sourced orders, a break-even and target-margin price, and today's schedule against the announced 1 October 2026 one — is ordinary arithmetic you can put in a spreadsheet. Getting there means reading the rates off Seller University yourself, building a formula that keeps commission out of a refund credit without also keeping it out of the cost side, and duplicating the whole sheet to hold a second schedule next to the first.

What does a spreadsheet not do that this calculator does?

Keep the organic-versus-affiliate split, the return rate, and the fee-schedule comparison on one screen without re-deriving the sheet each time a rate changes. The easiest mistake to make by hand is netting the affiliate commission back out of a returned order's cost — it is not: the creator keeps it. This calculator applies that rule the same way every time, computes a price that holds your margin, and produces a shareable link that carries the whole scenario instead of a file to keep in sync between two people.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, when your situation has a wrinkle this calculator does not model — a bundle of several SKUs in one order, a tiered commission that changes by volume, or a fee structure from a category or plan this tool's inputs cannot represent. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any rule you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right fields for one SKU moving through the organic-versus-affiliate, returns, and schedule-change decisions.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. A shareable link carries your numbers in the URL itself rather than sending them to a server, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your prices, costs, or creator rates.

what-will-the-tiktok-shop-fee-change-cos.text:
TIKTOK SHOP · ANNOUNCED FEE CHANGE

The headline is 6% to 8%. What it costs you depends on where the order came from.

The announced US schedule adds a creator facilitation rate on top of a higher referral — but facilitation lands on affiliate-sourced orders, not on the organic ones. A shop selling mostly organic is hit less hard than the headline implies, and a shop living on creator video is hit harder. This page puts your SKU through both schedules, then solves for the two things you can actually change: the list price and the unit cost. Back to the full calculator.

The listing

What the change costs this SKU

Order source Before After Costs you

What you can do about it

    Transparent arithmetic from your inputs — not TikTok’s live schedule, and not advice about what to charge. The announced rates are an announcement, not a guarantee they ship unchanged. Confirm your own referral, facilitation, and creator payout rules in Seller Center before you relist.

    Common questions

    What will the 1 October 2026 TikTok Shop fee change cost me?

    It depends on the SKU and on where the order came from. On the worked example — a $19.99 item, $4.99 shipping charged, 15% creator commission on item price only, 12% returns — the announced 8% referral plus 1.5% creator facilitation costs about $0.78 more on an affiliate-sourced order and about $0.45 more on an organic one. At 8 orders a day that is roughly $190 a month. Put your own numbers in the form to get your figure.

    Does the announced facilitation fee hit every TikTok Shop order?

    No. In this model the 1.5% creator facilitation applies to affiliate-sourced orders only, so a shop selling mostly organic is hit less hard than the headline suggests. The page splits the two so you can weight them by your own affiliate share instead of assuming one number covers the catalogue.

    How much do I have to raise my price to hold my margin?

    The page solves for it. It takes the expected margin your SKU earns under today's schedule, then finds the list price under the announced schedule that lands on that same margin after returns, creator commission, fulfillment, and ads. On the worked example a $19.99 listing needs about $21.94 to hold a 27.7% margin.

    Is raising the price the only option?

    No. The other lever is unit cost, so the page also shows the most the unit can cost and still clear, before and after. On the worked example that ceiling falls from about $11.73 to about $10.93 — which is the number to take to a supplier if the listing price cannot move.
